title: The Years the Locusts Ate
paragraphs:
The Years the Locusts Ate
The Astonishing Promise Hidden in Joel 2:25—and Why God’s Restoration Is Greater Than Your Greatest Loss
There are verses people quote.
And then there are verses people cling to when their world has fallen apart.
Joel 2:25 belongs to the second category.
It is the verse whispered by mothers who regret years they cannot get back.
It is the verse held tightly by fathers who feel they failed their families.
It is the verse bookmarked by believers who once burned brightly for Christ but drifted into seasons of compromise, addiction, bitterness, fear, rebellion, or spiritual apathy.
Because somewhere deep inside every human heart lives the same haunting question:
Can God restore what I destroyed?
Not simply replace it.
Not merely comfort me after it.
But restore it.
Can God redeem years?
Can He rewrite a story?
Can He do something so extraordinary that the ending becomes more beautiful than the beginning ever was?
The answer unfolds in one of the most breathtaking promises in all of Scripture.
The Lord declares:
“And I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust hath eaten...” (Joel 2:25, KJV)
At first glance, it sounds poetic.
But when we step into the world of Joel, we discover something far more powerful.
This promise was born from devastation.
It emerged from scandal.
It rose from judgment.
And ultimately, it points us directly to Jesus Christ—the One who rewrites everything.

The prophet Joel was speaking to the people of Judah after a catastrophic locust invasion. Entire harvests were destroyed. Fields were stripped bare. Vineyards were ruined. Economic stability vanished.
The Hebrew text uses the word וְשִׁלַּמְתִּי (ve-shillamti), translated “I will restore.”
But this word carries a richer meaning than many English readers realize.
It comes from the Hebrew root שָׁלַם (shalam).
This is the same root from which we get the word שָׁלוֹם (shalom).
Most people know shalom means peace.
Yet biblical peace is not merely the absence of conflict.
It means wholeness.
Completeness.
Things made right.
Things restored to their intended condition.
God is not merely promising replacement.
He is promising restoration toward wholeness.
He is declaring:
“I will make whole what was broken.”
That changes everything.
Because most of us know what it feels like to lose years.
Some lost years to addiction.
Some lost years chasing money.
Some lost years pursuing relationships that pulled them away from God.
Some lost years imprisoned by shame.
Some lost years hiding secret sins.
Some lost years simply surviving while their faith slowly cooled.
And sometimes the deepest pain is not what happened to us.
It is what happened because of us.
The opportunities missed.
The children neglected.
The marriages damaged.
The words spoken.
The trust broken.
The moments we would give anything to relive.
Those are the years that haunt us.
Those are the years the locusts ate.
Yet Joel's prophecy reveals something astonishing.
The locusts were not merely insects.
They became symbols of judgment, loss, destruction, and consequences.
The text mentions several kinds of locusts:
הָאַרְבֶּה (ha'arbeh) — the swarming locust.
הַיֶּלֶק (ha-yeleq) — the creeping locust.
הֶחָסִיל (hechasil) — the consuming locust.
הַגָּזָם (ha-gazam) — the cutting locust.
The imagery is intentional.
Wave after wave.
Loss after loss.
Destruction after destruction.
Just when people thought nothing more could be taken, another swarm arrived.
Isn't that how life often feels?
One disappointment comes.
Then another.
Then another.
A failed relationship.
A diagnosis.
A financial collapse.
A betrayal.
A prodigal child.
A moral failure.
A season of depression.
A spiritual drought.
And before long, it feels as though the field of your life has been stripped bare.
The enemy wants you to believe the story ends there.
God says otherwise.
Because Joel's promise was never primarily about agriculture.
It was about redemption.
It was about the character of God.
It was about a Father whose specialty is restoration.
Throughout Scripture, God repeatedly demonstrates this pattern.
Abraham waited decades for promises to unfold.
Joseph lost years in slavery and prison.
Naomi returned from Moab believing her story was over.
David fell into scandal and grief.
Peter denied Christ three times.
Paul persecuted believers.
Yet God transformed every story.
Not because the people were flawless.
But because God is faithful.
This theme reaches its climax in Jesus Christ.
The Gospel itself is the ultimate story of restoration.
Humanity rebelled.
Sin entered the world.
Creation fractured.
Death spread.
Hope seemed lost.
Then Jesus stepped into history.
The New Testament uses the Greek word ἀποκατάστασις (apokatastasis), meaning restoration or renewal.
In Acts 3:21, Scripture speaks of the future restoration of all things.
Jesus is not merely saving souls.
He is restoring creation.
Restoring relationships.
Restoring purpose.
Restoring what sin destroyed.
The cross is God's declaration that no ruin is beyond redemption.
Think about the scandal of grace.
Peter publicly denied Jesus.
Three times.
Around a charcoal fire.
Days later, Jesus restored him around another charcoal fire.
Not coincidence.
Redemption.
Thomas doubted.
Jesus restored him.
Mary Magdalene was tormented by demons.
Jesus restored her.
The thief on the cross wasted nearly his entire life.
Jesus restored him in his final hours.
This is who Christ is.
He walks into wreckage and creates redemption.
He enters ruins and builds testimonies.
He takes broken chapters and writes unexpected endings.
That is why Joel 2:25 resonates so deeply.
Because every human being knows what loss feels like.
But only the Gospel reveals a God who restores.
Notice something extraordinary.
The Lord does not merely say:
“I will restore your harvest.”
He says:
“I will restore your years.”
Years.
Time itself.
The thing no human can recover.
Money can return.
Health can improve.
Relationships can heal.
But time?
Once it passes, it never comes back.
Yet God specializes in accomplishing more through surrendered years than we could ever accomplish through decades of striving.
Some people spend twenty years running from God and then accomplish more for His kingdom in five surrendered years than they did in the previous twenty.
Not because time literally reverses.
But because grace multiplies.
The enemy wastes.
God redeems.
The enemy steals.
God restores.
The enemy scars.
God transforms scars into testimonies.
This does not mean consequences disappear.
Joel's audience still remembered the devastation.
David still carried consequences after his sin.
Peter never forgot his denial.
But redemption means the consequences no longer have the final word.
Jesus does.
That is the difference.
Many readers carrying regret need to hear this today.
You are not disqualified because of your past.
You are not unusable because of your failures.
You are not forgotten because of wasted years.
If God can redeem Peter's denial, He can redeem your failure.
If God can redeem Paul's persecution, He can redeem your past.
If God can redeem David's scandal, He can redeem your mistakes.
The Gospel is not merely forgiveness.
It is transformation.
It is restoration.
It is resurrection life invading dead places.
Perhaps that is why Joel's promise continues to echo across centuries.
Because every generation contains people standing in ruined fields wondering whether anything can grow again.
God's answer remains unchanged.
Yes.
Not because of human strength.
Not because of positive thinking.
Not because of self-improvement.
But because Jesus Christ still restores what sin, suffering, and brokenness have stolen.
And perhaps that is exactly where you find yourself today.
Looking over years you wish were different.
Carrying memories you wish could be erased.
Wondering whether God can still use what remains.
The answer of Joel 2:25 is not theoretical.
It is deeply personal.
The Lord who restored Peter.
The Lord who restored Naomi.
The Lord who restored Joseph.
The Lord who restored Israel.
Is the same Lord who still restores today.
Your story is not over.
The locusts do not get the final chapter.
Jesus does.
And when Jesus writes the ending, restoration becomes possible in places that once seemed hopeless.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
That is the beauty of grace.
That is the promise hidden inside Joel 2:25.
Not that God simply gives back what was lost.
But that He creates something so drenched in redemption that His glory shines brighter than the devastation ever did.
If this message stirred your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
What “locust years” has God been healing in your life?
The years may be gone, but in Christ, their purpose never has to be.
